slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: Used in routine screening of liver health and to help diagnose or monitor liver problems, usually as part of a liver function panel. Some liver diseases raise ALT before symptoms appear, so the test may help detect them early.

Ordered when there are symptoms of liver damage (for example jaundice, dark urine or light-colored stool, abdominal swelling or pain, frequent itching) or a high risk of liver damage: family history of liver disease, alcohol use disorder, obesity, diabetes, medicines that can harm the liver, or hepatitis or exposure to it.
ALT is usually measured together with AST in a liver function panel. Because ALT is found mostly in the liver, it checks more specifically for liver damage.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: ALT (alanine transaminase) is an enzyme found mainly in the liver, and its blood level is usually low. When liver cells are damaged, they release ALT into the bloodstream.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
bullets: High: Possible causes of liver damage with a high ALT: hepatitis, infection, cirrhosis, liver cancer, other liver diseases, a lack of blood flow to the liver, certain medicines (such as cholesterol or pain medicines) and poisons.

High: Cytolytic (hepatocellular) pattern: ALT and AST are raised disproportionately to alkaline phosphatase. It points to liver-cell injury; the work-up looks for viral hepatitis, fatty liver disease, alcohol, medicines and other causes.
Low: Low ALT is not common and may lead to further testing. Possible causes include vitamin B6 deficiency and chronic kidney disease.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Tell the provider about all medicines taken; some may need to be paused, but only on the provider's advice. Because ALT is usually ordered with other blood tests, fasting for several hours is often required.

Interferences: A high ALT does not always mean a condition that needs treatment. Age, sex, weight, certain medicines and dietary supplements, intense exercise and the phase of the menstrual cycle can affect the result.
Limitations: ALT is interpreted together with the other liver tests. It may help tell acute from chronic liver problems, but the ALT level does not reflect how much of the liver is damaged.

When liver test results are abnormal, the provider compares all the measured substances to look for patterns that suggest different types of liver conditions. Liver function tests alone usually cannot diagnose a specific disease.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
bullets: The liver’s synthetic function (hepatocellular failure pattern) is judged not by enzymes but by proteins the liver makes: albumin and prothrombin time (PT/INR); bilirubin also reflects the liver’s clearing work. A high ALT by itself does not mean liver failure.

slides.title: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: Part of routine screening of liver health; helps diagnose or monitor liver problems and may help diagnose other conditions. It may be ordered alone but is often part of a liver function panel.

Ordered at routine checkups, to monitor treatment of a liver problem, with symptoms of liver damage (such as jaundice, nausea, abdominal swelling or pain, dark urine), or without symptoms when liver disease risk is higher (family history, alcohol use disorder, obesity, diabetes, medicines that can harm the liver, hepatitis or exposure to it).

Physiology: AST (aspartate aminotransferase) is an enzyme found mainly in the liver, but also in the heart, muscles and other tissues. Its blood level is usually low; when the liver or other AST-containing cells are damaged, AST is released into the blood.

slides.title: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)
bullets: High: High AST may be due to liver disease or other liver problems. Other possible causes: hepatitis, cirrhosis, mononucleosis, heart procedures or problems, pancreatitis, hemochromatosis (too much iron), deep burns, seizures, use of drugs toxic to the liver (especially alcohol) and surgery.
High: ALT is often ordered together with AST. High AST and/or ALT may mean some type of liver damage.
High: AST rising with ALT out of proportion to alkaline phosphatase indicates a cytolytic (hepatocellular) pattern; if ALP predominates, a cholestatic pattern.
Low: Low AST levels in the blood are usually considered normal.

slides.title: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Tell the provider about all medicines taken; stop any only if the provider says so. AST is usually ordered with other blood tests, which often require fasting for up to 12 hours.
Interferences: A result outside the normal range does not always mean a condition that needs treatment. Pregnancy, exercise, certain medicines, age and sex can affect the result.

Limitations: When liver test results are abnormal, the provider compares all the measured substances to look for patterns that suggest different types of liver conditions. Liver function tests alone usually cannot diagnose a specific disease.

slides.title: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)
bullets: The De Ritis ratio is AST/ALT. Classically it is usually above 2 in alcoholic liver disease and below 1 in chronic viral hepatitis and chronic cholestasis; in non-alcoholic liver disease a ratio above 1 may suggest cirrhosis. With cirrhosis the ratio separates alcoholic from non-alcoholic causes less well. AST is also found in heart and muscle, so the ratio is meaningful only for liver conditions.

slides.title: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: Used to screen for or help diagnose liver and bone diseases and to help diagnose or monitor other conditions. Often done with a comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) or liver function tests, or when there are symptoms of liver damage or a bone disorder (bone pain, joint inflammation, unusually shaped or enlarged bones, broken bones).
Physiology: ALP is an enzyme present in all body tissues, with higher amounts in the liver, bile ducts and bones. Each part of the body makes a different type of ALP.

slides.title: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
bullets: High: High ALP from the liver may be a sign of bile duct blockage, cirrhosis, hepatitis or mononucleosis (which can sometimes cause swelling in the liver).

High: If ALP is high and liver tests are normal, a bone disorder such as Paget's disease of bone is possible. Moderately high ALP may occur with many conditions, including Hodgkin lymphoma, heart failure and certain infections; a high ALP may also occur without a condition that needs treatment.
High: Cholestatic pattern: alkaline phosphatase is raised out of proportion to ALT and AST. A raised GGT supports a liver source. If bilirubin rises too, bile-duct obstruction is considered.

Low: Low ALP is less common. Possible causes: zinc deficiency, protein deficiency, malnutrition, pernicious anemia, thyroid disease, Wilson disease and hypophosphatasia (a rare genetic disease affecting bones and teeth).

slides.title: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Tell the provider about all medicines taken; some may need to be paused, but only on the provider's advice. Because ALP is usually ordered with other blood tests, fasting for several hours is often required.

Interferences: Pregnancy can raise ALP, and children and teens may have high ALP because their bones are growing. Birth control pills and some medicines may lower ALP while others raise it, and a fatty meal before the test may cause a small increase.

Limitations: The ALP test alone cannot tell which tissue the ALP comes from, so other tests are usually needed. An ALP isoenzyme test can show its source (not available everywhere); if liver function tests are also high, the ALP is likely of liver origin.

slides.title: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
bullets: Abnormal liver test results don't always mean a liver problem: high ALP, for example, can be a sign of bone disease as well as liver disease. The provider also considers symptoms, medical history, liver disease risk and medicines taken.

slides.title: Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: Used to help diagnose liver disease, to tell liver disease from a bone disorder, to check for bile duct blockage, and to screen for or monitor alcohol use disorder. Drinking alcohol raises GGT, and most people with alcohol use disorder have high GGT.
Usually done with or after other liver tests, most often ALP. Both GGT and ALP may rise in diseases of the liver and bile ducts, but only ALP rises in bone disease.
Physiology: GGT is an enzyme found throughout the body but mainly in the liver. If the liver or bile ducts are damaged, GGT may leak into the bloodstream.

slides.title: Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)
bullets: High: High GGT may be a sign of liver damage. Possible causes include hepatitis, cirrhosis, alcohol use disorder, pancreatitis, diabetes, heart failure and medicine side effects. The result cannot show which condition is responsible, but usually the higher the GGT, the more liver damage.
High: Compared with ALP: high ALP with high GGT points to a liver disorder rather than a bone disorder, while high ALP with low or normal GGT makes a bone disorder more likely.
Low: A low or normal GGT means liver disease is unlikely.

slides.title: Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Ask the provider about specific instructions; fasting for a set time before the test may be requested.
Interferences: Results may be affected by certain medicines or supplements, drinking alcohol and smoking cigarettes. GGT levels go down after meals.

Limitations: GGT cannot identify the specific cause of liver disease; it only indicates that the liver is being damaged. The provider interprets it with symptoms, medical history and other blood tests.

Among liver laboratory patterns GGT belongs to the cholestatic group: rising with ALP supports a hepatobiliary cause, while a high ALP with normal GGT supports bone. GGT also rises with alcohol and some medicines, so alone it does not prove cholestasis.

slides.title: Total bilirubin
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood; heel-stick blood in newborns

What it is used for: Used to check liver health, look for the cause of jaundice, find a bile duct blockage, monitor existing liver disease and check how well treatment works. It also helps diagnose disorders in which red blood cells break down too quickly, such as hemolytic anemia.

Commonly used to help diagnose newborn jaundice. Many healthy babies get it because their liver is not yet mature enough; it is usually harmless and clears within a few weeks, but in some cases high bilirubin can lead to brain damage, so infants are often tested as a precaution.

slides.title: Total bilirubin
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Bilirubin is a yellowish substance formed during the normal breakdown of old red blood cells and is found in bile. A healthy liver removes most of it through the bile ducts; if the liver is damaged or the ducts are blocked, bilirubin can leak into the blood, and too much can cause jaundice.

Jaundice arises in three ways: too many red cells break down (prehepatic, haemolytic); the liver is damaged or cannot process bilirubin (hepatic); bilirubin from the liver cannot reach the gut (posthepatic, obstructive — blocked bile ducts).

slides.title: Total bilirubin
bullets: High: Possible causes of high bilirubin (hyperbilirubinemia): hemolytic anemia, liver disease and blockage of the bile ducts.

High: So a raised total bilirubin is fractionated. Mainly indirect (unconjugated) — haemolysis or impaired conjugation such as Gilbert syndrome; direct (conjugated) — hepatocellular disease (e.g., viral or alcoholic hepatitis) or cholestasis/bile-duct obstruction.
Low: Low bilirubin (hypobilirubinemia) is not usually a cause for concern; it may be due to medicines such as antibiotics, birth control pills, sleeping pills and seizure medicines.

slides.title: Total bilirubin
bullets: Pre-analytics: The provider may ask for fasting for several hours before the test. Tell the provider about all medicines taken; stop any only if the provider says so.
Interferences: An abnormal result does not always mean a condition that needs treatment: some medicines, certain foods and strenuous exercise can also raise bilirubin.

Limitations: Normal ranges vary between laboratories and with sex and age (infant or child). Bilirubin is only one measure of liver health; liver function tests, liver protein tests, urine tests, an ultrasound or a liver biopsy may also be needed.

When liver test results are abnormal, the provider compares all the measured substances to look for patterns that suggest different types of liver conditions. Liver function tests alone usually cannot diagnose a specific disease.

slides.title: Total bilirubin
bullets: Urine and stool help tell the types apart. Prehepatic: no bilirubin in urine (unconjugated bilirubin does not pass into urine), much urobilinogen, dark stool. Hepatic: bilirubin in urine, urobilinogen often raised. Posthepatic: bilirubin in urine (dark urine), little or no urobilinogen, pale clay-coloured stool. This is a general pattern — diagnosis relies on the clinical picture and other tests.

slides.title: Direct (conjugated) bilirubin
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood
What it is used for: Direct (conjugated) bilirubin is one of the names under which bilirubin blood testing is done, alongside total and indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin.
Bilirubin blood testing is used to check liver health, look for the cause of jaundice, find out whether the bile ducts are blocked and monitor existing liver disease.

Physiology: Bilirubin forms during the normal breakdown of old red blood cells and is found in bile. A healthy liver removes most of it through the bile ducts; if the liver is damaged or the bile ducts are blocked, bilirubin can leak into the blood.

slides.title: Direct (conjugated) bilirubin
bullets: High: Most bilirubin circulates unconjugated. A raised conjugated (direct) bilirubin in most settings implies hepatocellular disease or biliary obstruction/cholestasis; this fraction is water-soluble and passes into urine, so bilirubin appears in urine.

slides.title: Direct (conjugated) bilirubin
bullets: Pre-analytics: The provider may ask for fasting for several hours before the test. Tell the provider about all medicines taken; stop any only if the provider says so.

Limitations: Bilirubin results are only one measure of liver health, and normal values vary by laboratory, sex and age (infant or child). Other tests, such as liver function tests, urine tests or an ultrasound, may be needed.

The MedlinePlus encyclopedia gives less than 0.3 mg/dL (5.1 µmol/L) as an example normal for direct bilirubin, but the reference depends on the laboratory and method — use the range on the report. Healthy urine normally contains no bilirubin.

slides.title: Albumin
slides.eyebrow: Proteins and inflammation · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (serum)

What it is used for: Used to check general health and nutrition and how well the liver and kidneys work, and to monitor treatment of conditions that affect albumin. A damaged liver or poor nutrition can reduce albumin production, and damaged kidneys may let albumin pass into the urine. Often part of a liver panel or comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP).

Physiology: Albumin is a protein made by the liver. It keeps the fluid part of the blood from leaking out of blood vessels into tissues and carries hormones, vitamins and enzymes; with too little albumin, fluid can build up in the lungs, abdomen or elsewhere.

slides.title: Albumin
slides.eyebrow: Proteins and inflammation · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: High albumin may be a sign of dehydration, which can be caused by severe diarrhea or other conditions.

Low: Possible causes of low albumin: liver disease (including severe cirrhosis, hepatitis and steatotic liver disease), kidney disease, malnutrition (especially lack of protein in the diet), infection, digestive diseases that impair use of protein from food (such as Crohn's disease and malabsorption disorders), burns over a large area of the body and thyroid disease.

slides.title: Albumin
slides.eyebrow: Proteins and inflammation · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for albumin itself; fasting for several hours may be needed if other blood tests are ordered. Some medicines can affect the result, so tell the provider what is being taken.

Interferences: An out-of-range result does not always mean a condition that needs treatment. Steroids, insulin and hormones can raise albumin; not eating for 24–48 hours and some medicines, including birth control pills, can lower it, and albumin is lower during pregnancy.
Limitations: An albumin test alone cannot diagnose a condition; the provider usually interprets it together with other test results.

slides.title: Viral hepatitis B
bullets: CDC recommends screening all adults 18 and older at least once with a triple panel (HBsAg, anti-HBs, total anti-HBc), and testing for HBsAg in every pregnancy. Total anti-HBc is required to diagnose infection; the other markers show the type of infection and immunity.

slides.title: Viral hepatitis B
rows: Indicates infectiousness (may be transiently positive within 30 days after a vaccine dose).
Indicates recovery and immunity, or successful vaccination.
Previous or ongoing infection of undefined timing; lasts for life and is absent after vaccination alone.
Recent infection (within about 6 months); ordered only when acute infection is a concern.

slides.title: Viral hepatitis B
rows: Acute infection is likely — link to care.
Chronic infection is likely — link to care.
Resolved infection; counsel on reactivation risk.
Isolated anti-HBc: resolved infection with waned anti-HBs, occult infection, a false positive, or a mutant HBsAg missed by the assay — needs further evaluation.

slides.title: Viral hepatitis C
bullets: CDC recommends screening all adults 18 and older at least once and pregnant women during each pregnancy. First an HCV antibody test; if reactive, HCV RNA testing (which laboratories should run automatically).

slides.title: Viral hepatitis C
rows: Screening test. A reactive result may mean current infection, past resolved infection or a biologic false positive.
Identifies current infection: the diagnosis rests on detecting HCV RNA.

slides.title: Viral hepatitis C
rows: Current infection — counsel and link to care and treatment.
Anti-HCV reactive + HCV RNA not detected
No current infection (past infection or false positive); usually no further action.
No antibody detected. If recent exposure is suspected, test for RNA.

slides.title: Viral hepatitis C
bullets: Antibodies usually become detectable 8–11 weeks after infection, RNA within 1–2 weeks. With possible exposure in the past 6 months, RNA testing is recommended regardless of the antibody result. Before antiviral therapy, RNA is retested on a new sample.

slides.title: Fatty liver disease (MASLD/NAFLD)
bullets: Fat builds up in the liver. Overweight, insulin resistance or type 2 diabetes, high triglycerides and metabolic syndrome raise the risk. Diagnosis uses blood tests, imaging and sometimes biopsy; alcohol intake and other causes of liver fat are also assessed.

slides.title: Fatty liver disease (MASLD/NAFLD)
rows: Raised ALT and AST may lead the clinician to suspect MASLD.
Calculated from routine blood results; help identify or rule out advanced liver fibrosis.
Tests for other causes of raised liver enzymes
Additional blood tests for other conditions that can raise liver enzymes.

slides.title: Fatty liver disease (MASLD/NAFLD)
rows: ALT/AST ↑ + risk factors (obesity, type 2 diabetes, high triglycerides)
MASLD is possible — imaging and exclusion of other causes are needed.
Advanced fibrosis is possible — elastography; biopsy is sometimes recommended.

slides.title: Fatty liver disease (MASLD/NAFLD)
bullets: Routine imaging shows liver fat but not inflammation or fibrosis. Only a biopsy can prove MASH.

slides.title: Jaundice and cholestasis
bullets: Bilirubin leaks into the blood when the liver is damaged or the bile ducts are blocked, causing jaundice. Liver tests are compared with each other to find patterns that suggest a type of liver condition; on their own they usually cannot diagnose a specific disease.

slides.title: Jaundice and cholestasis
rows: To look for the cause of jaundice, find a bile duct blockage and monitor liver disease.
High ALP from the liver may point to blocked bile ducts, cirrhosis or hepatitis.
Helps tell where ALP comes from: both rise in liver and bile duct disease, only ALP in bone disease.
Part of the liver panel; the pattern of results points to the type of liver condition.

slides.title: Jaundice and cholestasis
rows: A liver or bile duct disorder is likely (not bone).
A bone disorder is more likely.
Possible causes: hemolytic anemia, liver disease or blocked bile ducts — other tests tell them apart.
Prehepatic (haemolytic): indirect bilirubin ↑, no urine bilirubin, urobilinogen ↑, dark stool
Haemolysis or impaired conjugation such as Gilbert syndrome; check haemolysis markers.
Hepatic: both fractions ↑, urine bilirubin present, urobilinogen often ↑, ALT/AST predominate
Hepatocellular injury (e.g., viral or alcoholic hepatitis, cirrhosis).
Posthepatic (obstructive): direct bilirubin ↑, urine bilirubin present, urobilinogen ↓ or absent, pale stool; ALP and GGT predominate
Bile-duct obstruction (stone, tumour, stricture) likely — imaging is needed.
ALT/AST raised out of proportion to ALP (cytolysis)
Typical of alcoholic liver disease; in non-alcoholic disease a ratio above 1 may suggest cirrhosis.

slides.title: Jaundice and cholestasis
rows: Reduced liver synthetic function (hepatocellular failure) likely.

slides.title: Jaundice and cholestasis
bullets: Bilirubin is only one measure of liver health: liver function tests, urine tests, ultrasound or a liver biopsy may also be needed. Abnormal liver tests do not always mean liver disease.

slides.title: Cytolysis (hepatocellular injury)
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Liver laboratory patterns
bullets: Markers: ALT and AST ↑ out of proportion to ALP
Meaning: Liver-cell injury: hepatitis, fatty liver, alcohol, medicines

slides.title: Cholestasis
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Liver laboratory patterns
bullets: Markers: ALP ↑ out of proportion to ALT/AST; GGT ↑ (liver source); direct bilirubin often ↑
Meaning: Impaired bile flow; ALP ↑ with normal GGT — think of bone

slides.title: Hepatocellular failure (synthetic function)
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Liver laboratory patterns
bullets: Markers: Albumin ↓, prolonged prothrombin time (PT/INR), bilirubin ↑
Meaning: The liver makes too little protein and clotting factors; a high ALT alone does not mean this

slides.title: De Ritis ratio (AST/ALT)
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Liver laboratory patterns
bullets: > 2: Usually alcoholic liver disease
< 1: Chronic viral hepatitis, chronic cholestasis
> 1 (non-alcoholic disease): May suggest cirrhosis
AST is also in heart and muscle — the ratio only makes sense for liver conditions.

slides.title: Prehepatic (haemolytic)
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Telling jaundice types apart
bullets: Blood bilirubin: Indirect (unconjugated) ↑
Urine bilirubin: Absent — this fraction does not enter urine
Urine urobilinogen: ↑
Stool: Dark
Causes: Haemolysis; impaired conjugation (Gilbert syndrome)

slides.title: Hepatic
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Telling jaundice types apart
bullets: Blood bilirubin: Both fractions ↑, including direct (conjugated)
Urine bilirubin: Present
Urine urobilinogen: Often ↑
Markers: ALT/AST predominate (cytolysis)
Causes: Viral or alcoholic hepatitis, cirrhosis, medicines

slides.title: Posthepatic (obstructive)
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Telling jaundice types apart
bullets: Blood bilirubin: Direct (conjugated) ↑
Urine bilirubin: Present (dark urine)
Urine urobilinogen: ↓ or absent
Stool: Pale, clay-coloured
Markers: ALP and GGT predominate (cholestasis)
Causes: Bile-duct stone, tumour, stricture

slides.title: Note
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Telling jaundice types apart
bullets: Jaundice arises in three ways: excess red-cell breakdown, liver damage, or bilirubin failing to reach the gut. This is a general scheme; diagnosis uses the clinical picture, imaging and other tests.

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits
slides.footnote: The reference interval varies by laboratory, method and population; the laboratory verifies its own interval (verification).

slides.title: A patient's ALT is markedly high. What does the ALT level itself tell you about how much of the liver is damaged?
options: The higher the ALT, the larger the share of the liver that has been damaged
Nothing reliable — the ALT level is not related to the extent of damage
A high ALT confirms that cirrhosis is the cause of the damage
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the ALT level does not reflect the extent of damage; it is interpreted together with the other liver tests.

Basis: MedlinePlus: the amount of ALT in the blood isn't related to how much the liver may be damaged; ALT is compared with the other liver tests.

slides.title: Why is ALT considered a more liver-specific marker of damage than AST?
options: ALT is found mostly in the liver, while AST is also found in the heart, muscles and other tissues
ALT is not affected by medicines, exercise or age, so any change in it reflects the liver alone
ALT is released only when liver cancer is present, so a high ALT points to a tumor rather than other damage
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: AST can also rise when tissues outside the liver are damaged, whereas ALT comes mainly from the liver.

Basis: MedlinePlus: ALT is mostly found in the liver and checks more specifically for liver damage; AST is also found in the heart, muscles and other tissues.

slides.title: A patient with no known liver disease has a high AST. Why might the AST come from outside the liver?
options: AST is made only by red blood cells, so any AST in the blood comes from them
AST is also found in the heart, muscles and other tissues and is released when they are damaged
AST rises only when the patient has eaten before the blood draw instead of fasting as instructed
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source also lists non-liver causes of high AST, such as heart problems, deep burns, seizures and surgery.

Basis: MedlinePlus: AST is found mainly in the liver but also in the heart, muscles and other tissues; damaged AST-containing cells release it into the blood.

slides.title: How is a low AST level in the blood usually interpreted?
options: As a sign of liver failure
As proof that the sample was collected incorrectly
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source states that low AST levels in the blood are usually considered normal.

Basis: MedlinePlus: low levels of AST in the blood are usually considered normal.

slides.title: ALP is high, but the other liver tests are normal. Which explanation does the source suggest?
options: A bile duct blockage is confirmed, even though the other liver tests are normal
The only explanation is an error in the laboratory measurement
A bone disorder, such as Paget's disease of bone, may be the cause
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: with high ALP and normal liver tests the problem may be a bone disorder; an ALP isoenzyme test can show the source.

Basis: MedlinePlus: if ALP is high and liver tests are normal, the problem may be a bone disorder such as Paget's disease of bone.

slides.title: A 14-year-old has a high ALP. Which factor from the source should be considered before assuming disease?
options: Children and teens may have high ALP because their bones are growing
Teens always have very low ALP, so this means liver failure
Age does not affect ALP, so a high value must mean bone or liver disease
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source names bone growth as a reason for high ALP in children and teens.

Basis: MedlinePlus: children and teens may have high ALP because their bones are growing.

Pigment metabolism. Bilirubin formation?
bullets: 1. 70–90% of bilirubin comes from the hemoglobin of aged erythrocytes: in macrophages heme oxygenase converts heme to biliverdin, and biliverdin reductase converts it to indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin; the rest comes from myoglobin, cytochromes and ineffective erythropoiesis.

2. Indirect bilirubin is insoluble in water and is transported in the blood bound to albumin to the liver; in the hepatocyte, with the participation of UGT1A1, it is conjugated with glucuronic acid (direct bilirubin) and excreted into the bile.
3. In the intestine bacteria convert it to urobilinogen; part is reabsorbed (urobilinogen in urine), the rest is converted to stercobilin and colors the stool.

slides.title: Pigment metabolism. Bilirubin formation?
bullets: 4. Disorders: hemolysis – indirect bilirubin rises; conjugation defects (Gilbert, Crigler-Najjar); hepatocellular injury – both fractions; cholestasis/obstruction – direct bilirubin, bilirubin in urine, stool becomes pale.
5. Laboratory: total and direct bilirubin (diazo reaction), indirect = total − direct; bilirubin and urobilinogen in urine; ALT/AST, ALP/GGT, hemolysis markers.

slides.title: Methods of determining bilirubin?
bullets: 1. The basic principle is the diazo reaction: bilirubin forms azobilirubin (colored) with diazotized sulfanilic acid; direct (conjugated) bilirubin reacts without an accelerator (caffeine-benzoate, etc.), total bilirubin with an accelerator (Jendrassik–Grof and its modifications).
2. Other methods: enzymatic/oxidative methods with vanadate or bilirubin oxidase; in newborns direct spectrophotometry (bilirubinometry) and transcutaneous measurement.
3. Indirect bilirubin is calculated: total − direct.
4. Preanalytics: bilirubin breaks down in light – keep the sample in the dark; interference from hemolysis and lipemia.

5. The reference interval depends on the laboratory, unit µmol/L (for example StatPearls: total bilirubin 2–17, direct 0–6 µmol/L; normally <1 mg/dL ≈ 17 µmol/L); interpret the result together with liver enzymes and hemolysis markers.

slides.title: Clinical and diagnostic significance of transaminases and methods of determination?
bullets: 1. ALT and AST are enzymes that transfer an amino group from an amino acid to α-ketoglutarate (coenzyme – pyridoxal phosphate, a derivative of vitamin B6).

2. Determination: kinetic UV method (IFCC reference procedure, 37 °C) – the product formed oxidizes NADH in a reaction with an auxiliary enzyme, and the decrease in absorbance at 340 nm is measured; historical colorimetric end-point methods are poorly standardized.
3. ALT is mainly in the liver – more specific for hepatocellular injury; AST in liver, heart, skeletal muscle, erythrocytes.
4. Interpretation: very high values – acute viral/toxic/ischemic hepatitis; AST:ALT >2 – alcohol-related injury; isolated AST elevation – muscle (compare with CK) or hemolysis.
5. Preanalytics: hemolysis falsely raises AST; physical exertion, some drugs.
